nameStory: The name 'chickweed' comes from the fact that chickens and other birds love to eat these small, tender plants. The 'field' part refers to this species' preference for open agricultural areas and disturbed soils. 'American' distinguishes it from the more common European chickweeds that have naturalized throughout New England.
description: American field chickweed is a small, low-growing annual herb that forms delicate mats close to the ground. This native wildflower typically reaches only 2-6 inches tall, with slender stems that often sprawl outward. It produces tiny white flowers with deeply notched petals that give them a star-like appearance. The entire plant has a soft, almost downy texture and tends to grow in patches rather than as individual specimens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers about 1/4 inch across with 5 deeply notched petals that look almost split in half, creating a 10-pointed star effect. The petals feel papery and delicate to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval to lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They're soft and slightly fuzzy, with a grayish-green color and no teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely growing more than 6 inches tall. The stems are weak and often lean on neighboring plants for support.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, cylindrical capsules that split open at the tip to release tiny, kidney-shaped brown seeds. The capsules make a barely audible crackling sound when ripe and dry.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant feels soft and slightly sticky due to fine hairs covering the stems and leaves. When crushed, it has a mild, fresh green scent.

habitat: American field chickweed thrives in disturbed soils of agricultural fields, garden edges, and roadsides throughout New England. It prefers sandy or loamy soils that are well-drained but not too dry. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in cultivated areas, particularly where the soil has been recently turned or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering by late April or May. The fresh green foliage is most noticeable as it contrasts with dormant grasses.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in early to mid-summer, with the tiny white star-flowers most visible on sunny days when they're fully open.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue producing flowers and seeds until the first hard frost. The foliage may take on slightly reddish tints in cool weather.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'American field chickweed,' this plant is so rare in New England that it's been documented only 6 times - making it far less common than its European cousins that have completely taken over our lawns and gardens!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common mouse-ear chickweed, but American field chickweed has much more deeply notched petals that almost look split in two, while common mouse-ear has shallower notches. Memory trick: 'American splits' - the American species has petals that look completely split.
contextualKnowledge: The rarity of this native species in New England highlights how introduced European chickweeds have largely outcompeted our native varieties. What most people think of as 'chickweed' in their yards is actually the non-native common chickweed or mouse-ear chickweed from Europe.
compareHints: American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base. Common mouse-ear chickweed has much shorter petal notches, while snow-in-summer is a much larger, more robust garden plant. Field chickweed (C. arvense) is perennial and taller, while American field chickweed is annual and stays close to the ground.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England.
Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance.
Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals.
